FINAL RESEARCH EVIDENCE AUDIT (synthesis of frozen artifacts; no new experiment)
==============================================================================

Frozen dataset integrity (verified from raw JSON):
  v1: {'scenarios': 5, 'runs': 250, 'invalid': 0}
  v2: {'scenarios': 5, 'runs': 250, 'invalid': 0}
  v3: {'scenarios': 5, 'runs': 250, 'invalid': 0}
  v5: {'scenarios': 5, 'runs': 300, 'invalid': 0}
  v6: {'scenarios': 1, 'runs': 60, 'invalid': 0}
  v4: {'standard': 50, 'periodic': 50, 'modes': 'linucb-standard + linucb-periodic'}
  aria2: {'runs': 50, 'version': 'aria2 version 1.37.0'}
  aria2_wallclock: {'runs': 10, 'version': 'aria2 version 1.37.0'}
  granularity_wallclock: {'runs': 10}

Experimental chain:
  [v1] 256 KiB, 4 baseline modes + standard LinUCB
      -> LinUCB selected ActionNone 100% (250/250 valid)
  [v2] 256 KiB + deterministic 5-action warm-up
      -> lock-in removed; only ~2 learned decisions/run (250/250 valid)
  [v3] 4 MiB, 6 modes incl. standard LinUCB
      -> 32-122 learned decisions; standard LinUCB still locks onto one arm (250/250 valid)
  [lock-in diagnosis] replay of frozen v3 through production LinUCB
      -> 4582/4582 actions replayed; posterior dominance + frozen unselected arms + capped bonus
  [periodic-exploration diagnostic] frozen-state replay, interval 0 vs 5
      -> unique arms 1.0-1.5 -> 5.0; forced arms receive posterior updates; dominant preference unchanged
  [live periodic benchmark (v4)] live download, standard vs periodic, 100 runs
      -> effective controller changes; posterior moves; in loss scenario greedy behavior changed
  [v5] 4 MiB six-mode unified benchmark, 300 runs
      -> periodic LinUCB coverage in one campaign; scenario-dependent
  [wall-clock infrastructure] server RateSchedule (time-based transition)
      -> transition at fixed elapsed time independent of request count
  [v6] wall-clock throttle 512KiB/s -> 4MiB/s after 1 s, 60 runs
      -> periodic LinUCB sustains concurrency ~3.9; standard still locks
  [aria2 old throttle] aria2 1.37.0, request-count throttle, 50 runs
      -> 4 x 1 MiB requests; request-count transition never benefits aria2
  [granularity study] internal 1 MiB/4C vs aria2, old throttle
      -> matched internal closely reproduces aria2 in 4/5 scenarios
  [aria2 wall-clock] aria2 under wall-clock throttle, 10 runs
      -> all 4 large requests begin before 1 s; none reaches 4 MiB/s
  [wall-clock matched control] internal 1 MiB/4C under wall-clock throttle, 10 runs
      -> same request shape; mean 2055.7 ms vs aria2 2129.7 ms (+3.6%)

Key verified numbers:
  lock-in replay: 4582/4582
  feature norm mean: 1.0066; bytes_transferred always 1.0: True
  horizon study sizes: [262144, 524288, 1048576, 2097152, 4194304]
  aria2 wall-clock runs with a post-1s request: 0/10
  matched wall-clock mean: 2055.7 ms; aria2 wall-clock mean: 2129.7 ms

Consolidated limitations:
  - Synthetic single-server controlled HTTP Range server (not a CDN/origin).
  - Controlled impairments (server throttle, netem latency/loss); not real consumer networks.
  - No real-Internet / last-mile deployment validation.
  - n=10 per cell; no random seeds in the framework.
  - Descriptive statistics only (mean/median/SD/95% t-CI); no significance testing.
  - One-step reward credit assignment is approximate under concurrency > 1.
  - The harness models no meaningful chunk-size performance tradeoff.
  - Periodic exploration is deterministic cycling, not learned exploration.
  - aria2 differs in request/connection management (1 MiB minimum split, keep-alive).
  - IDM was not evaluated (Windows-only; no Linux measurement path).
  - Decision horizon varies with adaptive chunk behavior (32-128 requests).
  - No fairness objective is implemented (no measurable signal).
  - No broad generalization claim is supported.

SUPPORTED CONCLUSIONS:
  - Periodic exploration breaks frozen-arm starvation [coverage only; not preference change]
  - Periodic exploration causes posterior adaptation [boundary/forced events; deterministic not learned]
  - Periodic exploration causes effective controller changes [scenario-dependent; deterministic exploration]
  - Request granularity explains a substantial portion of the original aria2 difference [residual ~74 ms unexplained]
  - Wall-clock throttling removes the request-count confound [removes the trigger coupling for all granularities; does not equalize downloaders]

NOT SUPPORTED BY CURRENT EVIDENCE:
  - Joint adaptation of concurrency and chunk size is novel [broad joint adaptation is established prior work]
  - LinUCB learns an optimal concurrency policy [no optimality or convergence shown]
  - LinUCB consistently improves performance [descriptive only; no superiority claim]
  - Chunk-size adaptation is successfully learned [unmodelled tradeoff; not evidence of optimization]
  - The internal downloader outperforms aria2 [descriptive; granularity/connection differences remain]
  - aria2 is inferior under consumer networks [no real-network deployment]
  - The controller generalizes to real consumer networks [no external validity established]
  - The method is fair to competing downloaders [fairness explicitly absent]
  - The system demonstrates RL-based adaptation [adaptation observed with deterministic periodic exploration, not learned exploration]
  - The current evidence establishes causal action effectiveness [temporal attribution approximate]

==============================================================================
FINAL RESEARCH NARRATIVE
==============================================================================

Problem: single-source HTTP Range downloads under volatile/constrained
consumer-style conditions, where a client must decide how many requests to run
concurrently and how large future chunk allocations should be, without
disrupting in-flight work.

Method: a modular downloader (rangetracker/fetcher/assembler/metrics,
concurrency and chunk-size controllers, a serialized policy runner) with four
deterministic baselines and a contextual-bandit (disjoint LinUCB) policy; a
controlled synthetic Range server with throttling/delay/failure knobs and a
wall-clock rate schedule; a reproducible experiment harness with per-decision
trajectories.

Evaluation: controlled scenarios (baseline, server-throttle, latency, loss,
combined) at 256 KiB and 4 MiB, plus a wall-clock-throttle scenario; 5- and
6-mode campaigns; a granularity study; and an aria2 1.37.0 external baseline.

LinUCB finding: the initial reward/observable design produced an ActionNone
lock-in; a deterministic warm-up fixed the "never tried" problem but standard
disjoint LinUCB then locked onto a single arm because unselected arms are never
updated and the UCB bonus is small relative to the reward scale (constant
bytes_transferred caps the bonus near alpha).

Periodic exploration finding: deterministic cycling every N decisions removes
frozen-arm starvation (unique arms 1 -> 5), forces posterior updates, and causes
effective controller changes; it does not generally change the dominant
preference, though behavior is scenario/schedule-dependent.

Wall-clock finding: making the rate transition time-based (not request-count)
removed the granularity/trigger coupling; under it, periodic LinUCB sustained
concurrency ~3.9 and matched the concurrency-adaptive controller, while standard
LinUCB still locked onto a no-op.

aria2 finding: aria2 issues 4 large (1 MiB) requests with max in-flight 4; under
both throttles all four start before any transition, so it never uses the higher
rate on this scenario. A granularity/parallelism-matched internal control
reproduces aria2 within ~4%, so request granularity/scheduling explains a
substantial part of the observed difference; the residual is not mechanistically
attributed, and no real-network or IDM claim is made.

Overall contribution: an unusually complete, reproducible evidence chain for a
specific, narrow question - how deterministic and contextual-bandit controllers
behave for concurrency/chunk control on a controlled synthetic server - including
an explicit diagnosis of bandit lock-in, a deterministic exploration correction,
a request-count-vs-wall-clock confound control, and an external granularity-matched
comparison. It does NOT establish broad novelty, optimality, real-network
generalization, chunk-size optimization, fairness, or superiority over aria2.
